first_impression.reaction: Googled 'short wedding vows' on the train. The intro is short and promises 20 examples grouped by tone, so I'm staying. But then I hit a legal section about an Australian Act with two big blockquotes before I get to a single vow. I'm in Singapore. I'd scroll past it fast, find the examples, screenshot two or three and bookmark the page. Not enquiring.

journey.quote: Below are 20 original examples, each written to be spoken in well under a minute, grouped by tone and occasion.
journey.reaction: Exactly what I searched for. I know what I'm getting.

journey.quote: A strong short vow needs only a name, one specific detail, two or three promises and a closing line.
journey.reaction: Handy formula, I get it in one line. But there's no actual example vow up here. Even one short one would have answered my search straight away.

journey.quote: Keep vows to 1 to 2 minutes each; every example here runs well under a minute, so read yours aloud and time it.
journey.reaction: Slightly confusing. The title says under one minute, the advice says 1 to 2 minutes. Which is it? Fine once I think about it, but I shouldn't have to.

journey.section: What words do you legally have to say when you marry in Australia?
journey.quote: I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law.
journey.reaction: Long legal quote, Australian law, and it's sitting between me and the examples. On a phone this is a lot of thumb-scrolling. I'm not marrying in Australia as far as I know. Skipping.

journey.quote: If you marry legally in another country, the legal wording follows that country.
journey.reaction: Fair and honest, at least it admits it's not the same everywhere. Only New Zealand is covered though, nothing for where I am.

journey.quote: Three promises. I will listen. I will laugh with you, often. And I will show up every day, especially the hard ones.
journey.reaction: Love this one. Short, real, doesn't sound like a greeting card. Screenshotting.

journey.quote: Our dog approved of you before I did, and she has excellent judgement.
journey.reaction: Made me smile on the train. The funny section is the one I'd send to my partner.

journey.section: What are some good short wedding vows?
journey.quote: Each of these is our own writing, and yours to adapt.
journey.reaction: Good, so these aren't copied off ten other sites. Makes the list feel worth bookmarking.

journey.section: How do you write a wedding vow in under a minute?
journey.quote: "I will make the coffee on weekdays" is more convincing than a promise about the stars.
journey.reaction: Practical and a bit funny. The fill-in-the-blanks template above it is genuinely useful too.

journey.section: How do you say your vows with confidence?
journey.quote: Under a minute feels long when you are standing there, and that is fine.
journey.reaction: Reassuring. Short section, easy to skim.

journey.quote: Our advice is 1 to 2 minutes each. Every example in this guide runs well under a minute, so read yours aloud and time it before the day.
journey.reaction: Same answer I already read twice. The FAQ repeats the takeaways rather than adding anything new.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how many words is a one-minute vow? The page says don't count words, but I'd still like a rough number.
What are the legal words if I marry in Singapore or somewhere other than Australia or New Zealand?
Do you plan weddings for couples outside Australia, and what does Wedded Concierge cost? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: As at November 2026, the form of the ceremony sits in section 45 of the Marriage Act 1961, and the celebrant's explanation sits in section 46.
turn_offs_found.why: The whole Australian legal section, with two long blockquotes, sits before the examples I came for, so the answer is buried below content that doesn't apply to me.

turn_offs_found.quote: A strong short vow needs only a name, one specific detail, two or three promises and a closing line.
turn_offs_found.why: Key Takeaways describe a short vow but don't show one, so there's no actual example in the first 100 words.

would_share_with: My partner: screenshots of example 8 and the 'Light and funny' set, plus the fill-in-the-blanks template

cta_reaction.quote: Your celebrant or registrar sets the words; the place, the guests and the travel are the bigger puzzle.
cta_reaction.why: I came for vow wording and don't know the brand. A planning service for venues and travel isn't what I'm after right now. Bookmark, not enquire.

top_3_changes: Put one complete short example vow (example 8 would do) in the Key Takeaways or first 100 words.
Move the examples section above the Australian legal section, or shorten the legal section and link out, so phone readers reach the vows faster.
Clear up the 'under one minute' title versus '1 to 2 minutes' advice, and give a rough word count for a one-minute vow.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Stayed in character as Priya (search visitor): intro, Key Takeaways, skim past legal section, examples, template, delivery tips, FAQ and CTA, on a phone
No invented brand facts; fees, non-Australian clients and other countries' legal wording placed in unanswered_questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored

open_questions.question: Is the legal section placed before the examples deliberately for the Australian audience? For a search visitor it delays the answer; weigh against other personas.

assumptions: Priya arrived from a Google search for 'short wedding vows' on her phone, does not know the brand and is based in Singapore.
No brand facts, prices or fees invented; gaps listed as unanswered.
She skimmed the legal section rather than reading it, and read the examples, template, delivery tips, FAQ and CTAs.
